name: Nora Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in farming country, rolling hills, dairy and grain, and our crew covers about thirty villages. We're at the depot by seven, coffee, the job list, and then out in the trucks. A lot of what we do is connections for farms, new barns, grain dryers, milking sheds, and fixing the lines when a tractor or a storm takes one down. I'm an apprentice, so I'm mostly on the ground, rigging, passing tools, and doing my first climbs with Henrik, who's been at it thirty years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tom and I had a dairy farm for fifteen years, his father's farm, and we sold it four years ago when milk prices fell and the debts got too big. It was the worst year of our lives, but we got through it with family and the church. I took this apprenticeship because I know farms and I wanted a steady wage. The hard part is the physical learning at my age, and the money, which is tight, with Tom driving a milk tanker now and two children and a mortgage on the house in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there we are, the world keeps turning. At the depot we'd laugh, and Henrik would say he told us so. I'd not post anything online, I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay the same, which is fine. I finish my apprenticeship, keep my job, and we keep slowly getting back on our feet after the farm. That's all I'm asking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with the apprenticeship, three years left. Maybe sell some eggs from the hens at the weekend, a little extra. And keep putting a bit aside when I can, though that's hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Grateful for steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I use one to help write the church newsletter, and once to help me understand a tricky part of the safety rules. It's useful, but I wouldn't let it tell me how to raise my children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest pressure on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, and getting the apprenticeship done. After the farm, we've got very little saved. Every month is careful.

S0.say: She'd say the world keeps turning, laugh with the crew as Henrik said he told them so, and post nothing online.
S0.think: Things stay the same, which is fine. I finish my apprenticeship, keep my job and keep slowly getting back on our feet after the farm.
S0.do: Carries on with her apprenticeship, which has three years left. Sells eggs from her hens at weekends and puts a little aside when she can.
S0.quote: It's useful, but I wouldn't let it tell me how to raise my children.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is still recovering from losing the family dairy farm four years ago, and steadiness is what she wants most. She uses AI now and then, for the church newsletter and safety rules, with clear limits. Faith and family carried her through before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, and you work with it, you don't whine about it. At the depot I'd say let's learn what we need to learn. With friends at church I'd say we look after each other, as we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried. I'm the junior and I'm still learning. But I think good, practical people will still be needed, and I intend to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the company what training is coming and get on it, if they pay. Use the AI tools a bit more to help me study. Save what I can, cut back on the extras, and keep the eggs going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. Like seeing the weather change over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've seen change hit farming. Does this feel similar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. When the big dairies came in with milking robots, small farms like ours couldn't keep up. We waited too long to change. I wouldn't make that mistake again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, we've been through worse. And he'd be right. Then he'd ask if the milk tankers will drive themselves, which is a fair question.

S1.say: She'd say change comes and you work with it rather than whining, tell the crew to learn what they need, and tell church friends they'll look after each other.
S1.think: I'd be a bit worried as the junior still learning, but good practical people will still be needed, and I intend to be one of them.
S1.do: Asks the company what training is coming and takes it if it's paid. Uses AI tools more to study, saves what she can, cuts extras and keeps selling eggs.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, like weather changing over the hill.
S1.quote: When the big dairies came in with milking robots, small farms like ours couldn't keep up. We waited too long to change.
S1.fieldNote: Nora links this scenario to losing the farm when robot milking gave big dairies the edge. She's determined not to wait too long again. Her stance is self-reliant: work with change, don't complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's prepared, and we'll have to rely on each other. At church I'd say we should organise, help families who lose work. I'd not blame anyone out loud, it doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. I'm an apprentice, two years isn't long enough to finish, and Tom's tanker job would be one of the first to go. We'd be back where we were after the farm, but worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Tom straight away and cut everything we can. Ring the bank about the mortgage early, we learned that with the farm. Sell more from the hens and the garden, and ask Tom's brother about work on his farm, if there's any. And lean on the church and family, the way we did before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake again, like the year we sold the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anna and Jakob?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that it'll be hard, but we've been through hard before and come out. Anna's thirteen and remembers the farm, she'd understand. Jakob would ask if we could get a goat, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we had to, for the children, but I'd rather family and church first. Handouts aren't a life. I'd want to be back working as soon as there was work.

S2.say: She'd say nobody's prepared so people must rely on each other, and urge her church to organise help for families who lose work. She wouldn't blame anyone out loud.
S2.think: It frightens me. Two years isn't enough to finish my apprenticeship, and Tom's tanker job would be among the first to go, so we'd be back where we were after the farm, but worse.
S2.do: Cuts spending with Tom straight away and calls the bank about the mortgage early, a lesson from the farm. Sells more eggs and garden produce, asks Tom's brother about farm work and leans on church and family, accepting government help only if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake as she did the year they sold the farm.
S2.quote: We'd be back where we were after the farm, but worse.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI would reopen the wound of losing the farm, with both Nora's and Tom's jobs exposed. She'd turn first to church and family, accepting government help only for the children. She chose not to blame anyone out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough to prepare, if you're sensible. At church I'd say let's help each other get ready, maybe share what we learn. At work I'd say take every course you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I finish my ticket and have a couple of years of proper pay. And it gives me time to learn something that's still needed. I think I'd be all right, if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, then ask the company about training to maintain or supervise the new robot crews. Save every extra bit, even a hundred a month. Grow the egg and garden business a little, maybe sell at the farmers' market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd have time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the robots, if it pays and it's steady. I grew up on a farm, I'm used to machines. I'd rather understand them than be scared of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to work with the robots, or away from them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd be scrambling. Five, I'd be planning. That's the difference with five years.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to prepare if you're sensible, urge her church to help each other get ready, and tell the crew to take every course.
S3.think: Five years means I finish my ticket, get a couple of years of proper pay and have time to learn something still needed. I'd be all right if I'm careful.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship, then asks the company about training to maintain or supervise robot crews. Saves even 100 a month and grows her egg and garden sales, perhaps at the farmers' market.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, with time to plan.
S3.quote: I grew up on a farm, I'm used to machines. I'd rather understand them than be scared of them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts Nora from scrambling to planning. Her farm background makes her comfortable with machines, and she'd aim to maintain or supervise robot crews. Her small egg business grows as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, there's no need to panic. At church and at work I'd say learn what you can, look after your family, help your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I think we'd be all right. I'd be qualified, I'd have learned the robot side, and the children would be grown. We might even have something saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, then take courses in robot maintenance within a few years. Save steadily, aiming for a few months' cushion. And help Anna and Jakob choose trades or studies that will still be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. It feels like something we can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty-three, maybe training others or checking the robot crews. The mortgage nearly paid. Maybe a few more hens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Anything that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The village. If everyone loses work, what happens to the church, the school, the shop? I'd worry about the community more than about us.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare without panic, and tell church and crew to learn what they can, look after family and help neighbours.
S4.think: With ten years we'd be all right: qualified, trained on the robot side, children grown and maybe something saved.
S4.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and takes robot maintenance courses within a few years. Saves steadily toward a few months' cushion and helps her children choose trades or studies that will still be needed.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, as if it can be managed.
S4.quote: If everyone loses work, what happens to the church, the school, the shop?
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Nora's worry shifts from her family to her village and church. She pictures training others or checking robot crews at 53. Her steady, practical faith in preparation fits this pace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Tom and I would both lose work at the same time, with nothing saved. What would help is proper apprenticeships, paid, for jobs that will still exist, and the company giving fair notice and a fair payout. And help for communities, not just people, so our villages don't die.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith and community. When we lost the farm, it wasn't the government that got us through, it was the church and family. That will matter more than ever if this happens.

headlineQuote: When we lost the farm, it wasn't the government that got us through, it was the church and family.
portrait: Nora Weber is a 43-year-old apprentice lineworker in dairy and grain country who took up the trade after she and her husband Tom sold his family's dairy farm four years ago. Tom now drives a milk tanker, they have two children and a mortgage, and every month is careful. She uses AI now and then, believes in working with change, and trusts church and family over government. She is calm when AI stalls, uneasy with gradual change, alarmed at AGI in two years when it would echo losing the farm, anxious at five and uneasy but hopeful at ten, when she sees a path into robot maintenance.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Tom would lose work at the same time with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships for jobs that will still exist, fair notice and payouts from the company, and help for communities so villages don't die.
